citeAs: Clark, C., Lee, K., Chang, M.-W., Kwiatkowski, T., Collins, M., & Toutanova, K. (2019). BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044.
creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova (Google AI Language, University of Washington)
description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of 16,000 naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the article title, and a yes/no answer. The questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and are paired with Wikipedia passages by human annotators.
name: BoolQ
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three of the authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality. Disagreements were resolved by mutual agreement to produce "gold-standard" labels. The answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the cases where annotations differed from gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process. First, they decide if the question is "good" (comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information), judged before seeing the Wikipedia page. Next, for good questions, annotators find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question, and can mark questions as "not answerable" if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information. Finally, annotators mark whether the question's answer is "yes" or "no". Examples are singly annotated.
rai:dataBiases: "Yes" answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set), creating a class imbalance. The dataset is drawn from Google search queries, which may reflect the demographics and interests of Google search users. Questions span topics including entertainment media, nature/science, sports, law/government, history, and fictional events.
rai:dataCollection: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results. The question and Wikipedia page are then given to a human annotator for further processing. 13k questions were gathered from this pipeline and combined with 3k yes/no questions from the NQ training set.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine that are likely yes/no questions, paired with Wikipedia pages returned as one of the first five search results. Additionally, 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set were incorporated.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset contains only yes/no questions, limiting its scope. The best model achieves 80.4% accuracy compared to 90% human accuracy, leaving a significant gap. The dataset analysis may be slightly out-of-date as the dataset was updated after the analysis was carried out. The dataset does not include document-level context, only passage-level.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions are heuristically filtered to identify yes/no questions by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words ({"did", "do", "does", "is", "are", "was", "were", "have", "has", "can", "could", "will", "would"}) and are of sufficient length. Only questions where a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five search results are kept. Questions are paired with the selected passage (not the entire document) to reduce ambiguity and keep input size manageable.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions, which is a common real-world information need. By using naturally occurring questions, the dataset avoids the artificial settings of engineered datasets and is more representative of real user needs.
rai:dataUseCases: Reading comprehension and natural language understanding, specifically yes/no question answering. The dataset is intended to test a model's ability to make complex inferences from text, including entailment-like reasoning. It is also intended as a benchmark for transfer learning approaches to NLP.

evidence.name: We build a reading comprehension dataset, BoolQ, of such questions, and show that they are unexpectedly challenging.
evidence.description: We follow the data collection method used by Natural Questions (NQ) to gather 16,000 naturally occurring yes/no questions into a dataset we call BoolQ (for Boolean Questions). Each question is paired with a paragraph from Wikipedia that an independent annotator has marked as containing the answer.

evidence.isLiveDataset: We split these questions into a 3.2k dev set, 3.2k test set, and 9.4k train set, ensuring questions from NQ are always in the train set.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries that are likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identiﬁed: we found selecting queries where the ﬁrst word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufﬁcient length, to be effective. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the ﬁrst ﬁve results, in which case the question and Wikipedia page are given to a human annotator for further processing.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the ﬁrst ﬁve results, in which case the question and Wikipedia page are given to a human annotator for further processing.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: We combine 13k questions gathered from this pipeline with an additional 3k questions with yes/no answers from the NQ training set to reach a total of 16k questions.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process. First, they decide if the question is good , meaning it is comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information. This judgment is made before the annotator sees the Wikipedia page. Next, for good questions, annotators ﬁnd a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question. Annotators can mark questions as "not answerable" if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information. Finally, annotators mark whether the question's answer is "yes" or "no".
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: First, in order to assess annotation quality, three of the authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples. If there was a disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement. We call the resulting labels "gold-standard" labels. On the 110 selected examples, the answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: Since the agreement was sufﬁciently high, we elected to use singly-annotated examples in the training/dev/test sets in order to be able to gather a larger dataset.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries that are likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identiﬁed: we found selecting queries where the ﬁrst word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufﬁcient length, to be effective. Note that, unlike in NQ, we only use questions that were marked as having a yes/no answer, and pair each question with the selected passage instead of the entire document.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: We build a reading comprehension dataset, BoolQ, of such questions, and show that they are unexpectedly challenging. They often query for complex, non-factoid information, and require difﬁcult entailment-like inference to solve.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: "Yes" answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set). The queries are typically short (average length 8.9 tokens) with longer passages (average length 108 tokens).
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: Note the dataset has been updated since we carried out this analysis, so it might be slightly out-of-date. Future work could include building a document-level version of this task, which would increase its difﬁculty and its correspondence to an end-user application.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: they can be used to construct highly inferential reading comprehension datasets that have the added beneﬁt of being directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions.
